reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: Phlegmasia alba dolens ('painful white leg', 'milk leg') is a severe form of acute iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis in which massive venous outflow obstruction produces a swollen, painful, pale limb; it is classically described postpartum but occurs with any cause of extensive proximal thrombosis
The pallor reflects tense subcutaneous oedema together with reflex arterial spasm, while patent collateral veins still permit some venous drainage, distinguishing it from the later cyanotic stage

The condition lies on a continuum: untreated progression to phlegmasia cerulea dolens (a cyanotic, near-total venous occlusion involving the collaterals) and then to venous gangrene threatens both the limb and life
Peripheral pulses are typically preserved in phlegmasia alba dolens, which helps differentiate it from acute arterial occlusion where the limb is likewise pale and painful
Massive fluid sequestration into the affected limb can precipitate hypovolaemia and circulatory compromise, and severe swelling may cause a compartment syndrome

Management centres on prompt therapeutic anticoagulation, limb elevation and consideration of catheter-directed thrombolysis or venous thrombectomy, alongside a search for underlying causes such as May-Thurner iliac vein compression or occult malignancy

It is a limb- and life-threatening emergency requiring urgent vascular assessment; venous gangrene carries a high risk of amputation and significant mortality and is strongly associated with malignancy and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
reference.pathophysiology: Extensive thrombosis of the iliofemoral venous segment obstructs venous outflow from the limb. In the alba stage the collateral veins remain patent, so the limb is pale, tensely swollen and painful, and reflex arterial vasospasm contributes to the pallor and to diminished distal perfusion. As thrombus propagates to involve the collateral and microvascular beds (phlegmasia cerulea dolens), venous drainage fails almost completely; capillary and venular pressures rise steeply, the limb becomes cyanotic and severely swollen, and large volumes of fluid sequester into the tissues, causing hypovolaemia. The resulting rise in tissue pressure, together with progressive microvascular thrombosis, impairs arterial inflow and can culminate in venous gangrene.
additionalDifferentials: Acute arterial occlusion (embolic or thrombotic limb ischaemia)
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound to confirm and localise the venous thrombosis
CT or MR venography to define the iliocaval extent and identify compressive lesions such as May-Thurner
Assessment of arterial perfusion (ankle pressures and Doppler) to exclude arterial occlusion
Full blood count with serial platelet monitoring for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and a coagulation profile
Renal function and metabolic screen given fluid sequestration and possible tissue injury
Evaluation for underlying malignancy and, where appropriate, thrombophilia
Compartment pressure assessment and markers of tissue injury if gangrene or compartment syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Progression to cyanosis (phlegmasia cerulea dolens) or to skin blistering and gangrene
Absent distal pulses or other signs of arterial compromise
Tense swelling suggesting an evolving compartment syndrome
A falling platelet count suggesting heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
reference.prognosis: With prompt anticoagulation and thrombus removal the white-leg stage can resolve, but progression to venous gangrene carries high rates of amputation and mortality. Long-term post-thrombotic syndrome is common in survivors, particularly after extensive iliofemoral thrombosis.
pitfalls: Mistaking the pale, painful limb for acute arterial ischaemia and delaying anticoagulation
Underestimating fluid sequestration and failing to resuscitate the circulation
Missing an underlying iliac vein compression or occult malignancy
Continuing heparin despite thrombocytopenia when heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is driving the thrombosis
